caption_hook: Pennsylvania has frozen magma, coal that still burns underground and one of the first leg-walkers.

layers.name: GETTYSBURG DIABASE
layers.hook: Molten rock that froze in place
layers.what: As Pangaea cracked apart, hot magma pushed into the red rock beneath southern Pennsylvania and cooled into hard, dark diabase. It weathers into huge, rounded boulders.
layers.bonus: Soldiers took cover behind these boulders at Devil's Den in the 1863 battle.

layers.name: LLEWELLYN FORMATION
layers.what: Tropical swamp forests were buried, then squeezed until they turned into anthracite, the hardest and cleanest-burning coal. The Pennsylvanian Period is named for this state.
layers.bonus: The Centralia mine fire has smoldered underground since 1962.

layers.name: CATSKILL FORMATION
layers.hook: Red mud and the first leg-walkers
layers.what: Muddy red floodplains and slow rivers once ran here. In that rock, scientists found Hynerpeton, one of the earliest four-limbed animals to crawl from water.
layers.bonus: Its shoulder bones came from a road cut near Hyner, found in 1993.

layers.name: MARCELLUS SHALE
layers.hook: Black mud rich in natural gas
layers.what: A deep, oxygen-poor sea once trapped dead plankton in black mud on the seafloor. Over time it turned into a shale that holds enormous amounts of natural gas.
layers.bonus: It helped make Pennsylvania the second-biggest natural gas state, after Texas.

layers.name: CHICKIES QUARTZITE
layers.hook: Beach sand turned to glass-hard rock
layers.what: Sand from an ancient beach was cemented into quartzite, one of the toughest rocks around. Today it forms steep cliffs high above the Susquehanna River.
layers.bonus: Chickies Rock Park gives wide views of the river from the top.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.hook: Gneiss from a lost mountain range
layers.what: Old gneiss and granite lie under Pennsylvania's younger layers and surface in the Reading Prong near Reading. They are the roots of a mountain range from over a billion years ago.
layers.bonus: Reading Prong rock carries natural uranium, a known source of radon in nearby homes.
